meta.title: GATE CSE Discrete Mathematics - Master Question Bank
meta.note: Append-only. Never delete previous entries. Historical PYQs carry verified provenance only; anything unverified is marked as such.

verified_pyqs.paper: GATE CSE 2023 (official CS paper, IIT Kanpur)
verified_pyqs.note: Geetha's conjecture: which options imply forall x (P(x) => exists y Q(x,y)).

verified_pyqs.paper: GATE CSE 2015 (listed as Set 1 Q18 by ExamSIDE and Set 2 Q3 by GATE Overflow)
verified_pyqs.note: Corrupt / kind / elected inference chain; answer: 'If a person is kind, he is not known to be corrupt'.

questions.source: Original practice question (AI-generated GATE-style) - not an official GATE question
questions.question: To disprove the statement  ∀n∈ℤ, P(n),  which of the following is logically correct AND sufficient?
options: Exhibit one integer n for which P(n) is false.
Prove that P(n) is true for every integer n.
Prove that P(n) is true for at least one integer n.
Prove that P(n) is false for every integer n.

solution.concept: The negation of a universal statement is an existential statement: ¬(∀n P(n)) ≡ ∃n ¬P(n).
steps: A universal claim is false as soon as a single instance fails.
Such a failing instance is a counterexample.
So one integer n with ¬P(n) is both necessary and sufficient to disprove ∀n P(n).
solution.misconception: Many students think a universal statement can only be refuted by proving the opposite for all n, or by finding a counterexample that is 'typical'. One valid counterexample is enough.
solution.takeaway: Remember: disprove ∀ with one ∃-counterexample; disprove ∃ by showing ∀¬ (no example exists).

questions.source: Original practice question (AI-generated GATE-style) - not an official GATE question
questions.question: The contrapositive of the implication  "If n² is even, then n is even"  is:
options: If n is even, then n² is even.
If n² is odd, then n is odd.
If n is odd, then n² is odd.
If n is even, then n² is odd.

solution.concept: The contrapositive of p → q is ¬q → ¬p, and it is logically equivalent to the original.
steps: Here p = "n² is even", q = "n is even".
¬q = "n is odd", ¬p = "n² is odd".
Contrapositive: "If n is odd, then n² is odd".
solution.misconception: Option (B) is the inverse ¬p → ¬q, which is equivalent to the converse, not the original. Students often swap contrapositive and inverse.
solution.takeaway: Contrapositive = negate both, then swap. Inverse = negate both, keep order. Converse = swap only.

questions.source: Original practice question (AI-generated GATE-style) - not an official GATE question
questions.question: The statement  "p is sufficient for q"  is formally written as:

solution.concept: Sufficient condition = the antecedent of the implication. Necessary condition = the consequent.
steps: "p is sufficient for q" means: the truth of p guarantees the truth of q.
That is exactly p → q.
solution.misconception: Confusing 'sufficient' with 'necessary'. p sufficient for q is p→q; p necessary for q is q→p.
solution.takeaway: Sufficient sits on the left of →; necessary sits on the right.

questions.source: Original practice question (AI-generated GATE-style) - not an official GATE question
questions.question: The standard proof that √2 is irrational begins by assuming √2 = a/b with gcd(a,b) = 1 and derives that both a and b are even. This is an example of:

solution.concept: In a proof by contradiction we assume the negation of the claim and derive an impossibility.
steps: Assume the negation: √2 is rational, √2 = a/b in lowest terms.
Derive a = 2m and b = 2n, so gcd(a,b) ≥ 2.
This contradicts gcd(a,b) = 1, so the assumption is false.
solution.misconception: Students sometimes call this a 'contrapositive' proof. It is a contradiction proof: we assume the opposite of the whole statement, not the negation of the conclusion of an implication.
solution.takeaway: Rationality of √2, infinitude of primes, and √2 + √3 irrationality are all classic contradiction proofs.

questions.source: Original practice question (AI-generated GATE-style) - not an official GATE question
questions.question: To prove a statement of the form  p ↔ q,  it is necessary and sufficient to prove:
options: both p → q and q → p

steps: A biconditional is the conjunction of the two implications.
Hence both directions must be established.
One may also build a chain of equivalences p ↔ r₁ ↔ r₂ ↔ q.
solution.misconception: Proving only one direction is a common error; a one-way proof does not establish 'if and only if'.
solution.takeaway: 'iff' proofs: prove 'necessary' and 'sufficient' (or 'only if' and 'if') separately.

questions.source: Original practice question (AI-generated GATE-style) - not an official GATE question
questions.question: For the statement  "If x > 3, then x² > 9",  which of the following is its CONVERSE?
options: x > 3 if and only if x² > 9.

solution.concept: Converse of p → q is q → p.
steps: Converse = q → p = "If x² > 9, then x > 3".
solution.misconception: Option (B) is the inverse and (C) is the contrapositive. A converse is not logically equivalent to the original.
solution.takeaway: Converse swaps; inverse negates; contrapositive does both. Only the contrapositive is equivalent.

questions.source: Original practice question (AI-generated GATE-style) - not an official GATE question
questions.question: Consider the statement:  "For every real number x, if x² = 4, then x = 2."  Which of the following correctly assesses it?

solution.concept: A universally quantified implication fails if some x makes the hypothesis true and the conclusion false.
steps: Take x = −2. Then x² = 4 (hypothesis true) but x ≠ 2 (conclusion false).
So the statement is false.
solution.misconception: x = 4 does not satisfy x² = 4, so it is not a counterexample — students often pick any 'unusual' value without checking the hypothesis.
solution.takeaway: Always verify a counterexample actually satisfies the hypothesis before using it.

questions.source: Original practice question (AI-generated GATE-style) - not an official GATE question
questions.question: Which of the following is a VALID rule of inference?
options: From p → q and q, infer p.
From p → q and p, infer ¬q.

solution.concept: Modus tollens: (p → q) ∧ ¬q ⇒ ¬p is valid. Affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent are fallacies.
steps: (A) affirms the consequent — invalid.
(B) denies the antecedent — invalid.
(C) modus tollens — valid.
(D) contradicts modus ponens — invalid.
solution.misconception: The two most common fallacies are 'affirming the consequent' and 'denying the antecedent'; both look like modus ponens/tollens but are invalid.
solution.takeaway: Valid: modus ponens, modus tollens, hypothetical syllogism, disjunctive syllogism, resolution.

questions.source: Original practice question (AI-generated GATE-style) - not an official GATE question
questions.question: To prove  "if n is an integer and n² is odd, then n is odd",  the cleanest standard approach is:
options: A direct proof expanding n² as a general integer.
Proof by contrapositive: assume n is even and show n² is even.

solution.concept: When the conclusion is hard to use directly, prove the contrapositive instead.
steps: Contrapositive: if n is even, then n² is even.
Let n = 2k; then n² = 4k² = 2(2k²), which is even.
Done.
solution.misconception: A direct proof of the original is awkward because 'n² odd' is hard to unpack; the contrapositive makes the algebra trivial.
solution.takeaway: If the hypothesis is a 'negative' or awkward property (odd, irrational, not divisible), try the contrapositive.

questions.source: Original practice question (AI-generated GATE-style) - not an official GATE question
questions.question: The phrase  "a is necessary for b"  is logically equivalent to:

solution.concept: 'a is necessary for b' means b cannot hold without a, i.e. b → a.
steps: If a were absent, b could not occur.
So b ⇒ a, written b → a.
solution.misconception: Reading 'necessary' as the antecedent. Necessary = consequent side: b → a.
solution.takeaway: Necessary = 'only if'. 'b only if a' is b → a.

questions.source: Original practice question (AI-generated GATE-style) - not an official GATE question
questions.question: Consider the statement:  "For every real number x, x² > x."  Which of the following is a correct disproof?

solution.concept: x² > x fails exactly when 0 ≤ x ≤ 1.
steps: So the statement fails for every x in [0,1].
x = 0.5 gives 0.25 > 0.5, which is false — a counterexample.
solution.misconception: Choosing a value such as x = 2 (which satisfies the inequality) instead of a failing value.
solution.takeaway: Solve the inequality first; the complement of its solution set is exactly where counterexamples live.

questions.source: Original practice question (AI-generated GATE-style) - not an official GATE question
questions.question: Consider the statement:  "For every real number x, if x² < 0, then x = 7."  Which of the following is correct?
options: False, because x = 7 does not satisfy x² < 0.
Vacuously true, because no real x satisfies x² < 0.

solution.concept: An implication p → q is true whenever the hypothesis p is false. If p is never true, the universal statement is vacuously true.
steps: For every real x, x² ≥ 0, so x² < 0 is false for all x.
Each implication instance is therefore true (false → anything is true).
Hence the universally quantified statement is (vacuously) true.
solution.misconception: Judging the statement 'false' because the conclusion 'x = 7' seems unrelated; the hypothesis is never satisfied, so the implication never fails.
solution.takeaway: Empty-domain / impossible-hypothesis implications are vacuously true — a favourite GATE trap.

questions.source: Original practice question (AI-generated GATE-style) - not an official GATE question
questions.question: Which of the following statements is most naturally proved by a proof by cases (division into cases)?
options: There are infinitely many prime numbers.

solution.concept: A proof by cases splits the domain into exhaustive sub-cases and proves the claim in each.
steps: |n| ≥ n: if n ≥ 0 then |n| = n ≥ n; if n < 0 then |n| = −n > n.
Both cases cover all integers, so the claim holds.
solution.misconception: Choosing √2 irrationality (contradiction) or infinitude of primes (contradiction) — those are not naturally case proofs.
solution.takeaway: Whenever a statement depends on the sign or residue of an integer, a case split (parity, sign, mod k) is usually cleanest.

questions.source: Original practice question (AI-generated GATE-style) - not an official GATE question
questions.question: A student wishes to disprove the claim  "Every odd integer greater than or equal to 5 can be written as a sum of three primes."  The logically correct strategy is to:
options: exhibit one odd integer ≥ 5 that cannot be written as a sum of three primes.
prove the claim for all odd integers ≥ 5.
exhibit an odd integer less than 5 that is not a sum of three primes.

solution.concept: A claim of the form ∀n≥5 (odd(n) → S(n)) is refuted by one qualifying counterexample inside the stated range.
steps: The claim quantifies over odd integers ≥ 5.
Disproof requires one odd integer ≥ 5 violating S(n).
A value below 5 is outside the domain and cannot refute the claim.
solution.misconception: Using an out-of-domain value (e.g. n = 1 or 3) as a 'counterexample'. It must satisfy every hypothesis of the claim.
solution.takeaway: A counterexample must lie inside the quantified domain AND satisfy the hypothesis.

questions.source: Original practice question (AI-generated GATE-style) - not an official GATE question
questions.question: Which of the following statements about proof techniques is FALSE?
options: A proof by contrapositive of p → q is a direct proof of ¬q → ¬p.
Proof by contradiction can be used for statements that are not implications.
If a statement is proved by contradiction, then its negation is false.
The inverse ¬p → ¬q of p → q is logically equivalent to p → q.

solution.concept: p → q is equivalent to its contrapositive ¬q → ¬p, but NOT to its inverse ¬p → ¬q.
steps: (A) True: that is the definition of a contrapositive proof.
(B) True: contradiction is general (e.g. 'there are infinitely many primes').
(C) True: deriving a contradiction shows ¬S is impossible, so S holds.
(D) False: ¬p → ¬q ≡ q → p, the converse, not p → q.
solution.misconception: Believing the inverse is equivalent to the original. Only the contrapositive is equivalent.
solution.takeaway: Equivalent to p→q: itself, its contrapositive. NOT equivalent: converse, inverse.

questions.source: Original practice question (AI-generated GATE-style) - not an official GATE question
questions.question: Which of the following are logically equivalent to  p → q ?  (Select all that apply.)

steps: Material implication: p → q ≡ ¬p ∨ q.
Contrapositive: p → q ≡ ¬q → ¬p.
Negation of conjunction: ¬p ∨ q ≡ ¬(p ∧ ¬q).
¬p → ¬q ≡ p ∨ ¬q ≡ q → p, the converse — not equivalent.
solution.misconception: Including (B): the inverse is equivalent to the converse, not to the original implication.
solution.takeaway: Memorise the three equivalent rewrites of an implication; the inverse is never one of them.

questions.source: Original practice question (AI-generated GATE-style) - not an official GATE question
questions.question: Which of the following statements are TRUE?  (Select all that apply.)
options: Every proof by contrapositive of p → q can also be phrased as a proof by contradiction.
Every proof by contradiction is a proof by contrapositive.
A proof by contrapositive of p → q proceeds by proving ¬q → ¬p directly.
A proof by contradiction of p → q may assume both p and ¬q and derive a contradiction.

solution.concept: Contrapositive is a special, direct way of doing what contradiction does indirectly.
steps: (A) True: assume p and ¬q, the contrapositive derivation gives a contradiction.
(B) False: contradiction applies to non-implication statements too.
(C) True: that is the definition.
(D) True: assuming p and ¬q is the standard contradiction setup for an implication.
solution.misconception: Thinking the two methods are identical. Contrapositive is strictly a proof of ¬q → ¬p; contradiction is more general.
solution.takeaway: Contrapositive ⊂ contradiction: every contrapositive proof is a contradiction proof, not vice versa.

questions.source: Original practice question (AI-generated GATE-style) - not an official GATE question
questions.question: Let S be the statement:  "If a positive integer is divisible by 6, then it is divisible by 3."  Which of the following are TRUE?  (Select all that apply.)
options: The converse of S is true.
The inverse of S is true.
The contrapositive of S is true.

solution.concept: S is true; its contrapositive is always equivalent to it; the converse and inverse need not be true.
steps: S: 6 | n ⇒ 3 | n. True, since 3 | 6.
Contrapositive: 3 ∤ n ⇒ 6 ∤ n. True (equivalent to S).
Converse: 3 | n ⇒ 6 | n. False, e.g. n = 9.
Inverse: 6 ∤ n ⇒ 3 ∤ n. False, e.g. n = 9.
solution.misconception: Assuming that if an implication is true then its converse is too. Converse and inverse can both fail.
solution.takeaway: Test converse/inverse with a small counterexample (here n = 9).

questions.source: Original practice question (AI-generated GATE-style) - not an official GATE question
questions.question: Consider the claim  C: "For every integer n, n² + n is even."  Which of the following are VALID ways to establish C?  (Select all that apply.)
options: Proof by cases: consider n even and n odd separately.
Proof by contradiction: suppose n² + n is odd and derive a contradiction.
Rewrite n² + n = n(n + 1) and note one of two consecutive integers is even.

solution.concept: Parity of n² + n can be shown by cases, by contradiction, or by a product-of-consecutive-integers argument.
steps: (B) Valid: n = 2k → n²+n = 2(2k²+k); n = 2k+1 → n²+n = 2(2k²+3k+1).
(C) Valid: assuming odd leads to n(n+1) odd, impossible for consecutive integers.
(A) Invalid: n = 2 satisfies C, it is not a disproof.
(D) Valid: of n and n+1 one is even, so the product is even.
solution.misconception: Thinking a single verified example (n = 2) 'proves' or 'disproves' a universal claim. Examples never prove a universal statement.
solution.takeaway: n² + n is always even — a template result worth memorising for parity arguments.

questions.source: Original practice question (AI-generated GATE-style) - not an official GATE question
questions.question: Which of the following statements are TRUE?  (Select all that apply.)
options: If p → q is true, then its converse q → p must also be true.
'p is necessary for q' is equivalent to q → p.
If p → q and q → r are both true, then p → r is true.
p ↔ q is true exactly when p and q have the same truth value.

solution.concept: Necessity, hypothetical syllogism, and the truth condition for a biconditional.
steps: (B) True by definition of a necessary condition.
(C) True: hypothetical syllogism (transitivity of →).
(A) False: an implication does not force its converse.
(D) True: ↔ is true precisely when both sides agree.
solution.misconception: Treating → as symmetric. Only ↔ is symmetric; → is not.
solution.takeaway: Chain implications freely (transitivity); never reverse a single implication without proof.

questions.source: Original practice question (AI-generated GATE-style) - not an official GATE question
questions.question:
Let p → q be a true implication that is NOT a biconditional. Among its converse, its inverse and its contrapositive, how many statements are logically equivalent to p → q?
(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: Only the contrapositive is logically equivalent to p → q.
steps: Converse q → p: not equivalent.
Inverse ¬p → ¬q: not equivalent.
Contrapositive ¬q → ¬p: equivalent.
Count = 1.
solution.misconception: Counting the converse and inverse as equivalent. They are equivalent to each other, not to p → q.
solution.takeaway: Of the three derived forms, exactly one (the contrapositive) is always equivalent.

questions.source: Original practice question (AI-generated GATE-style) - not an official GATE question
questions.question:
Consider the polynomial f(n) = n² + n + 41. Find the SMALLEST positive integer n for which f(n) is NOT prime.
(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: f(n) = n² + n + 41 is prime for n = 0..39 (Euler's polynomial) but fails at n = 40.
steps: Test the boundary n = 40: f(40) = 1600 + 40 + 41 = 1681.
1681 = 41², which is composite.
For n = 1..39, f(n) is prime, so 40 is the smallest positive n that fails.
solution.misconception: Stopping the search early and assuming the pattern continues; a single counterexample is decisive, but you must find the smallest one.
solution.takeaway: Euler's n²+n+41 is the classic 'looks always prime' trap; it first fails at n = 40.

questions.source: Original practice question (AI-generated GATE-style) - not an official GATE question
questions.question:
How many of the following four propositions are tautologies?
  (i)  p → (p ∨ q)
  (ii) (p ∧ q) → p
  (iii)(p → q) → (q → p)
  (iv) (p → q) ↔ (¬p ∨ q)
(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: A tautology is true for every truth assignment; use the truth table or algebraic equivalences.
steps: (i) p → (p∨q): when p is true p∨q is true; when p is false the implication is true. Tautology.
(ii) (p∧q) → p: if p∧q true then p true. Tautology.
(iii)(p→q)→(q→p): p = F, q = T gives (T)→(F) = F. Not a tautology.
(iv)(p→q)↔(¬p∨q): both sides are the same formula, so it is always true. Tautology.
Tautologies: (i), (ii), (iv) = 3.
solution.misconception: Marking (iii) as a tautology because both components 'look like implications'. Test p = F, q = T.
solution.takeaway: (iv) is an instance of the equivalence p→q ≡ ¬p∨q, so it is a tautology by definition.

questions.source: Original practice question (AI-generated GATE-style) - not an official GATE question
questions.question:
Consider the conjecture:  "For every integer n ≥ 2, the number 2ⁿ − 1 is prime."  How many counterexamples n exist with 2 ≤ n ≤ 10?
(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: 2ⁿ − 1 is prime only for certain n (Mersenne primes); composite values are counterexamples.
steps: n = 2: 3 (prime)
n = 3: 7 (prime)
n = 4: 15 = 3·5 (counterexample)
n = 5: 31 (prime)
n = 6: 63 = 3·21 (counterexample)
n = 7: 127 (prime)
n = 8: 255 = 3·5·17 (counterexample)
n = 9: 511 = 7·73 (counterexample)
n = 10: 1023 = 3·11·31 (counterexample)
Counterexamples: n = 4, 6, 8, 9, 10 → 5.
solution.misconception: Forgetting that 2ⁿ − 1 can be prime for some n and composite for others; each composite case counts.
solution.takeaway: If n is composite, 2ⁿ − 1 is composite; but n = 9 (odd composite) and n = 10 also fail here, so check each value.

questions.source: Original practice question (AI-generated GATE-style) - not an official GATE question
questions.question:
Consider the proposition  (p ∨ q) → (p ∧ q).  Over the four possible truth assignments of (p, q), how many make this proposition TRUE?
(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: An implication is false only when the antecedent is true and the consequent is false.
steps: (T,F): T → F = F.
(F,T): T → F = F.
(F,F): F → F = T.
True for 2 assignments.
solution.misconception: Assuming (F,F) is false. A false antecedent makes the implication vacuously true.
solution.takeaway: (p∨q) → (p∧q) is true exactly when p and q agree — i.e. it is equivalent to p ↔ q.
